strengths: Addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaboration affects interactive qualitative coding. Comparing topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM labeling across two contrasting corpora provides useful empirical breadth.
Separating consistency, cohesiveness/distinctiveness, and assignment correctness is valuable. Document-overlap and semantic measures capture different aspects of coding outcomes.

The study includes substantial human evaluation: researcher participation, 1,200 manually assessed document-theme pairs, dual annotation with adjudication, and reported agreement. Interviews add useful observations about control and usability.

The system descriptions are generally clear, and shared initial partitions help control starting conditions within systems. Appendices provide prompts, several computational settings, and detailed corpus analyses.
weaknesses: The design does not isolate collaboration timing. Section 4 compares individual coders with three-person teams, without evaluating consolidation of asynchronous work. Team size, available expertise, and potentially total effort therefore vary alongside synchrony. Reused participants always complete asynchronous sessions first, introducing possible learning effects. The evidence supports an exploratory comparison of individuals and teams more directly than conclusions about synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

The statistical support for the central claim is inadequate as reported. Tables 1–2 use unpaired t-tests with only two synchronous and three asynchronous codebooks per system, but do not identify test sample sizes or explain dependence among themes, document pairs, codebook comparisons, and reused participants. Treating these observations as independent would overstate precision. Analysis respecting the experimental units, uncertainty estimates, and clarification of multiple comparisons are needed before accepting the claimed significant effects.

The evaluation framework needs stronger validation. Independent maximum-similarity matching permits many-to-one theme alignments and depends on theme number and granularity, which are not reported. Centroid similarities near 0.98 coexist with low document overlap, yet there is no human validation that these semantic matches represent equivalent themes. Embedding cohesion alone does not establish the interpretive quality of a qualitative codebook.

Correctness evaluation is insufficiently specified and partly misinterpreted. Figure 4 reports F1, but Section 5.3 describes judgments of assigned document-theme pairs without defining recall, negative cases, or aggregation. Uncertainty estimates are absent, and only COVID results are assessed. The claim that asynchronous topic modeling is more accurate also conflicts with the figure: full-dataset scores are equal, and synchronous scores are higher at intermediate cutoffs. Treatment of unlabeled outputs, reaching 16.1% for one LLM run, also needs clarification.

Important reproducibility details remain unresolved. The stated total of 15 experiments is not reconciled with evaluating two datasets and five runs per system. Participant/session allocation, resulting theme counts and codebooks, the exact SBERT checkpoint, LLM decoding settings, and Climate-specific configurations are insufficiently documented. Promising a future code and annotation release does not resolve these gaps in the submitted evidence.

Several recommendations exceed the observations. Two corpora differing simultaneously in domain, size, length, and repetitiveness cannot establish which characteristics explain collaboration effects. Some Climate cohesiveness gains are only 0.01 despite being described as substantial. General conclusions about LLM scalability rest on one 3B model and prompting setup, while interview participant counts and analysis procedures are unspecified. These conclusions should be narrowed to the tested conditions.
